es.summary: Pérdida involuntaria de orina que puede ser de tipo estrés, urgencia o mixto. Afecta la calidad de vida y se maneja con medidas conductuales, farmacológicas y, en algunos casos, quirúrgicas.
key_points: Identificar tipo (estrés, urgencia, mixto) guía el tratamiento
Ejercicios del suelo pélvico son la base del manejo no farmacológico
Antimuscarínicos (p. ej., oxibutinina) se usan en incontinencia de urgencia
Factores de riesgo incluyen embarazo, menopausia, obesidad y tos crónica

pathophysiology: Debilidad del músculo del esfínter uretral y soporte del suelo pélvico
Aumento de presión intraabdominal supera la presión uretral
Desplazamiento de la vejiga o uretra altera el cierre uretral
risk_factors: Obesidad y aumento de presión abdominal
Tos crónica, asma o rinitis alérgica
signs_symptoms: Pérdida de orina al toser, estornudar o levantar peso
Urgencia súbita con goteo antes de llegar al baño
diagnostics: Historia clínica y diario de micción (volumen, episodios)
Prueba de estrés (carga con agua y tos)
Ecografía de residuo postmiccional (PVR) <50 mL normal
Uroflujometría y estudio urodinámico si se sospecha causa compleja
Análisis de orina para descartar infección
treatment: Ejercicios de Kegel y entrenamiento del suelo pélvico
Modificación de líquidos (evitar irritantes, limitar cafeína)
Cirugía de sling uretral para incontinencia de estrés
complications: Dermatitis e irritación cutánea por humedad
Impacto psicológico: ansiedad, depresión, aislamiento social
Incontinencia fecal asociada en casos de daño neurológico
nursing_care: Evaluar patrón de micción y tipo de incontinencia
Inspeccionar piel perineal cada 2 h y registrar irritación
Mantener posición semisentado para facilitar vaciado
Cambiar absorbentes cada 2 h o cuando estén saturados
Registrar volumen de pérdida y factores desencadenantes
Fomentar ejercicios de suelo pélvico antes y después de la micción
patient_teaching: Realizar ejercicios de Kegel 3 veces al día, 10 repeticiones cada una
Limitar ingesta de cafeína y alcohol; beber 1,5‑2 L de agua al día
Ir al baño cada 2‑3 h, incluso sin urgencia
Mantener higiene perineal de adelante hacia atrás
Usar ropa interior absorbente y cambiarla rápidamente

evidenced_by: Fuga de orina al caminar o subir escaleras
Fatiga al realizar actividades de la vida diaria
outcomes: Nivel de actividad: paciente aumentará tolerancia a la actividad realizando caminatas de 15 min sin fuga en 2 semanas
Control de la fuga: paciente reportará ≤1 episodio de fuga durante actividades diarias en 1 semana

interventions.action: Evaluar nivel de actividad y registrar episodios de fuga antes y después de la intervención
interventions.rationale: Permite establecer línea base y medir progreso

interventions.action: Enseñar técnica de respiración y contracción del suelo pélvico antes de iniciar actividad física
interventions.rationale: Reduce presión intraabdominal y previene la fuga

interventions.action: Programar descansos breves cada 10‑15 min durante actividades prolongadas
interventions.rationale: Evita fatiga y sobrecarga del esfínter

interventions.action: Reforzar ejercicios de Kegel 3 veces al día
interventions.rationale: Mejora fuerza del esfínter y control de la vejiga

interventions.action: Monitorear signos vitales y nivel de cansancio durante la actividad
interventions.rationale: Detecta intolerancia temprana y previene caídas

outcomes: Sin signos de infección urinaria (ausencia de fiebre, disuria, leucocitos en orina) durante la hospitalización

interventions.action: Mantener higiene perineal con agua tibia y secado suave después de cada episodio de fuga
interventions.rationale: Reduce colonización bacteriana

interventions.action: Cambiar absorbentes o pañales cada 2 h o cuando estén saturados
interventions.rationale: Previene humedad prolongada que favorece el crecimiento bacteriano

interventions.action: Fomentar ingesta adecuada de líquidos (≥1,5 L/día) salvo contraindicación
interventions.rationale: Promueve lavado de vías urinarias y disminuye bacterias

interventions.action: Observar y registrar temperatura, dolor al orinar y cambios en el color de la orina
interventions.rationale: Detección temprana de infección

interventions.action: Educar al paciente sobre signos de infección urinaria y cuándo buscar ayuda
interventions.rationale: Facilita intervención oportuna

en.summary: Unintentional loss of urine that can be of the stress, urgency, or mixed type. It affects quality of life and is managed with behavioral measures, pharmacologic therapy, and, in some cases, surgical interventions.
key_points: Identify type (stress, urgency, mixed) to guide treatment
Pelvic floor exercises are the foundation of non‑pharmacologic management
Antimuscarinics (e.g., oxybutynin) are used for urgency incontinence
Risk factors include pregnancy, menopause, obesity, and chronic cough

pathophysiology: Weakness of the urethral sphincter muscle and pelvic floor support
Increased intraabdominal pressure exceeds urethral pressure
Bladder or urethral displacement alters urethral closure
risk_factors: Chronic cough, asthma, or allergic rhinitis
Neurologic diseases (multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury)
signs_symptoms: Urine loss when coughing, sneezing, or lifting weight
Sudden urgency with dribbling before reaching the bathroom
diagnostics: Medical history and voiding diary (volume, episodes)
Uroflowmetry and urodynamic study if a complex cause is suspected
treatment: Kegel exercises and pelvic floor training
Urethral sling surgery for stress incontinence
complications: Dermatitis and skin irritation from moisture
Psychological impact: anxiety, depression, social isolation
Falls from rushing to the bathroom
Associated fecal incontinence in cases of neurologic damage
nursing_care: Assess voiding pattern and type of incontinence
Inspect perineal skin every 2 h and document irritation
Maintain semi‑upright position to facilitate emptying
Change absorbents every 2 h or when saturated
Encourage pelvic floor exercises before and after voiding
patient_teaching: Perform Kegel exercises 3 times daily, 10 repetitions each
Limit caffeine and alcohol intake; drink 1.5‑2 L of water daily
Use the bathroom every 2‑3 h, even without urgency
Maintain perineal hygiene from front to back
Use absorbent underwear and change it promptly

evidenced_by: Urine leakage when walking or climbing stairs
Fatigue during activities of daily living
outcomes: Activity level: patient will increase tolerance to activity by walking 15 min without leakage in 2 weeks
Leak control: patient will report ≤1 leakage episode during daily activities in 1 week

interventions.action: Assess activity level and record leakage episodes before and after intervention
interventions.rationale: Establish baseline and measure progress

interventions.action: Teach breathing technique and pelvic floor contraction before starting physical activity
interventions.rationale: Reduce intraabdominal pressure and prevent leakage

interventions.action: Schedule brief breaks every 10‑15 min during prolonged activities
interventions.rationale: Prevent fatigue and sphincter overload

interventions.action: Reinforce Kegel exercises 3 times daily
interventions.rationale: Improve sphincter strength and bladder control

interventions.action: Monitor vital signs and fatigue level during activity
interventions.rationale: Detect early intolerance and prevent falls

outcomes: No signs of urinary infection (absence of fever, dysuria, leukocytes in urine) during hospitalization

interventions.action: Maintain perineal hygiene with warm water and gentle drying after each leakage episode
interventions.rationale: Reduce bacterial colonization

interventions.action: Change absorbents or diapers every 2 h or when saturated
interventions.rationale: Prevent prolonged moisture that favors bacterial growth

interventions.action: Encourage adequate fluid intake (≥1.5 L/day) unless contraindicated
interventions.rationale: Promote urinary tract flushing and reduce bacteria

interventions.action: Observe and record temperature, pain during urination, and urine color changes
interventions.rationale: Early detection of infection

interventions.action: Educate patient on signs of urinary infection and when to seek help
interventions.rationale: Facilitate timely intervention

key_points.0.quote: Understanding the specific type of urinary incontinence, whether functional incontinence , mixed urinary incontinence , overflow incontinence , stress urinary incontinence , or urge urinary incontinence , is crucial for tailoring appropriate interventions ( Table 26.6 ).

key_points.2.quote: Anticholinergic medications, such as oxybutynin, may be prescribed to treat urge urinary incontinence and mixed urinary incontinence.

sections.risk_factors.0.quote: Are female, especially after going through pregnancy, childbirth, and/or menopause

sections.risk_factors.4.quote: It can also happen in some neurological conditions , such as multiple sclerosis and spinal cord injuries .

sections.signs_symptoms.0.quote: This could be due to coughing, sneezing, laughing, lifting something heavy, or physical activity.

sections.signs_symptoms.3.quote: The procedure aims to relieve symptoms of BPH, such as difficulty urinating, frequent urination, and incomplete bladder emptying.

sections.signs_symptoms.4.quote: Regular cleansing and gentle drying of the skin are paramount to prevent moisture-related dermatitis .

sections.diagnostics.0.quote: When assessing a patient for urinary retention, healthcare providers may inquire about the frequency and volume of urination , the presence of straining during voiding, and any associated pain or discomfort.

sections.diagnostics.2.quote: Normal PVR volume is typically between 50 and 100 mL.

sections.treatment.0.quote: Pelvic muscle exercises (also known as Kegel exercises) work the muscles used to stop urination, which can help prevent stress incontinence.

sections.treatment.1.quote: The process involves creating a voiding schedule, gradually extending the time between bathroom visits, and implementing strategies to suppress the urge to urinate.

sections.treatment.2.quote: Losing weight, drinking less caffeine (found in coffee, tea, and many sodas), preventing constipation, and avoiding lifting heavy objects may help with incontinence.

sections.treatment.5.quote: For women, a ring or a tampon-like device inserted into the vagina.

sections.complications.0.quote: Moisture-related dermatitis, often referred to as moisture-associated skin damage, is a skin condition characterized by inflammation and irritation resulting from prolonged exposure to moisture.

sections.complications.2.quote: Incontinence can lead to isolation and depression as people, embarrassed by the condition, limit their activities and social interactions.

sections.nursing_care.0.quote: It is also essential to assess fluid intake, voiding patterns, and the presence of other contributing factors, such as neurological conditions or medications.

sections.nursing_care.4.quote: The voiding diary should include the following: when and how much the patient urinates urinary leakage and what the patient was doing when it happened (e.g., running, biking, laughing) sudden urges to urinate how often the

sections.patient_teaching.2.quote: Timed voiding can be used to help a patient regain control of their bladder by urinating on a set schedule (e.g., every hour) whether they feel the urge to urinate or not.
